processing: Steamed to stop oxidation, hand-rolled, then pan-worked in stages to straighten and tighten the strips, and finished with a slow low-heat drying. Shaping in the pan is the step that gives the tea its form.
harvest_season: Picked young at one bud and one barely opened leaf; spring is normally the prized picking for a tender green like this, though the exact dates are not well recorded.
appearance_dry: Straight, tight, rounded dark-green strips with sharp tips and a full coat of white down.
appearance_wet: Tender, even buds and young leaves that spread out and stay bright.
taste_profile: A clean, fresh aroma over a full and brisk body, with a sweetness that lingers after the swallow.

brewing.notes: Water at 85-90 °C suits it. The down clouds the first cup slightly, which is normal for a downy tea.

vintage_note: Sold as a recent-harvest green tea and best drunk fresh; it is not a tea to keep for years. Age is not part of its value, so a recent production date matters more than anything else on the pack.
description:
Yunhai Baihao, cloud-sea white tip, is a modern named green tea from Menghai in southern Yunnan. It takes its name from the mist that sits over the growing area and from the white down on the leaf. It shows what big-leaf Yunnan bushes can do outside pu-erh.

It is unusual in being steamed and then finished by hand in a pan. After steaming and rolling comes a series of low-heat stages that pull, straighten and rub the strips tight, and then a long, gentle drying that builds aroma.

The cup is yellow-green, fresh and fairly strong, closer to a brisk Yunnan green than a delicate eastern one, with a sweet aftertaste. Use water around 85-90 °C and watch the strips spread out in a glass. Long steeps bring out the briskness of the large leaf.

Look for straight, downy, sharp-tipped strips. Buy for the appearance and for a clear production date.
history:
The tea was created in the early 1970s by the Tea Research Institute of the Yunnan Academy of Agricultural Sciences, which is based in Menghai county. The Ministry of Commerce named it a national famous tea in 1986.

The recorded recipe uses two clonal varieties, the provincial Changye Baihao and the national Yunkang 14.
